projectDesc.p: The Welte-Mignon Advertisements Collection brings together print advertisements for the Welte-Mignon reproducing piano that appeared between 1905 and 1930. It was created as part of the PhD project "Grünfelds Geist" at the University of Tübingen, which considers piano rolls as objects of a digital edition. The collection is published at https://anz.welte225.org.

samplingDecl.p: The collection gathers print advertisements for the Welte-Mignon reproducing piano that appeared between 1905 and 1930 and were published by M. Welte & Söhne, by one of its licensees, or by a dealer or agent selling the instrument. Each advertisement is encoded once; its further printings, in the same or in other periodicals, are listed as further sources.

The advertisements were found in digitised newspapers and magazines: Chronicling America (Library of Congress), the British Newspaper Archive, HathiTrust (copies of the Universities of California, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota and Virginia), the Internet Archive, the Digitale Sammlungen of the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, ANNO (Austrian National Library), the International Arcade Museum Library, Georgia Historic Newspapers, Delpher (KB, National Library of the Netherlands), eluxemburgensia (National Library of Luxembourg), RetroNews (Bibliothèque nationale de France), the archives of Le Temps, the Nasjonalbiblioteket of Norway, Mediestream (Royal Danish Library), the National Library of Latvia (through Europeana), Canadiana, the Hemeroteca Nacional Digital de México, the St Petersburg State Theatre Library, Trove (National Library of Australia), the newspapers of the Kungliga biblioteket of Sweden, e-newspaperarchives.ch, BAnQ numérique (Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec), the Biblioteca Virtual de Prensa Histórica, the archive of ABC, ARCA (Biblioteca de Catalunya) and Polona (National Library of Poland).

editorialDecl.p: Each file transcribes one printing of an advertisement, the one whose scan its facsimile zones refer to; decls on text points to its sourceDesc. The further printings were identified as the same advertisement but not collated word for word; differences that were noticed are recorded with app, whose first rdg is that of the transcribed printing, or in a note. A printing that was set anew counts as the same advertisement as long as its text differs only in spelling, punctuation, a few words or a sentence; its note describes the setting, whose line breaks and type are not recorded.

The regions and lines of the scans were mostly marked in eScriptorium and converted from PAGE XML to TEI. The text was in part recognised automatically (HTR) and corrected against the scan, in part transcribed by hand. The advertisements published outside Germany, the United Kingdom and the United States, and a few from Germany, were transcribed from the scans, encoded, given their regions by Claude, an AI model; their revision history says so. Until the editor has checked such an advertisement against the scan, status on its revisionDesc is unchecked; that of every other advertisement is checked. The topics of all advertisements were assigned by Claude.

correction.p: Errors of the original are not corrected but marked with sic.

normalization.p: Spelling and punctuation follow the original and are not normalised. Text set in capitals is often transcribed in mixed case and marked with the rendition #uc.

hyphenation.p: Hyphens at the end of a line are kept as printed.

segmentation.p: Every region of the original page is a div that points to its zone in the facsimile with facs. The lines of the original are marked with lb; the typography is recorded with rendition. The zones refer to the first graphic of a surface, the scan they were drawn on. Where the holding library serves the page through IIIF, a second graphic of the type IIIF gives that image and its size.

interpretation.p: Parts of an advertisement that concern other products than the Welte-Mignon are not transcribed but marked with gap, which describes them in a desc. Illustrations are described in figure. Persons are linked to the GND with corresp; firms are linked to the GND or, where it has no record of them, to Wikidata. Recurring arguments and motifs are marked as topics with ana on seg and figure, pointing to the taxonomy of topics. The taxonomy was induced by Claude in four blind readings of all advertisements, each in a different order and without knowledge of the editor's earlier taxonomy, which it replaced in October 2026; it keeps the topics that at least three of the readings found. The topics are an interpretation, assigned by whom resp says, so far all by Claude; the editor has not yet checked them.

stdVals.p: Dates of publication are given in ISO 8601 in when, as precisely as they are known.

taxonomy.desc: Topics: the recurring arguments and motifs of the advertisements, in their texts and in their pictures

category.desc: The ad claims that the playing of the artist is reproduced exactly, faithfully, naturally or completely, as "the actual playing" of the pianist. A bare "reproduces the playing of …" without such a qualifier does not count.
The ad names what is kept beyond the notes: touch, phrasing, pedalling, dynamics, tempo, shading, tone colour, or the individuality and characteristic style of each pianist.

The instrument is said to capture the soul, spirit, feeling or inner life of the performer, a spiritual register beyond the technical one of touch and nuance ("the living soul of the artist", "Musikseele").
The instrument is set apart from mechanical, automatic or player- piano playing: it is human, artistic, "not a surrogate", or the prejudice that it is mechanical is refuted.
The listener feels that the artist is present or seated at the instrument ("as if he sat at your piano", "close your eyes"), or cannot tell the reproduction from the live artist.
The playing is preserved for ever or for future generations; the artists become immortal, and dead artists still play.
The instrument is called a wonder, miracle, marvel or magic, or it causes astonishment, disbelief or speechlessness.
The absent performer appears as a phantom or spirit: ghostly or semi-transparent hands and figures, keys moving with no one seated, the artist summoned at will ("zitieren", "summon").
The reader is challenged to verify the claims by listening, comparing or testing ("must be heard to be believed", "hear it in comparison"). A bare invitation to a demonstration does not count.

category.gloss: The great pianists in your home
category.desc: The famous pianists can be heard in your own home or on your own piano, at any time, as often as you wish, at your command ("The Master's Fingers on Your Piano", concerts at home).
A private, comfortable scene: the fireside, an armchair, lamplight, the family gathered, a quiet evening, in the text or in the picture.

The instrument is famous and admired throughout the world, acclaimed by all great artists, critics or the press, adopted by conservatories and other institutions, or decorated with medals and prizes. The bare epithet "the famous Welte-Mignon" does not count.
Royalty, the nobility or the court appear as listeners, owners or patrons, including titles of purveyor to the court ("Hoflieferant").
The instrument is framed as an invention: epoch-making, ingenious, the greatest of the age, a sensation, the newest thing.
The instrument is called perfect, the best, the finest, supreme or unsurpassed, or the culmination of a line of progress.
The instrument is "the only one", the standard for all others, it surpasses its rivals or has nothing in common with them, or the reader is warned against cheap or unknown makes.
The Welte-Mignon is the original or the first reproducing piano, protected by the original patents; the history of the Welte firm and its founders guarantees it.

The ad explains or shows the technology: the recording process, the pneumatic or electric mechanism, the roll, the drive from a light socket, or it likens the recording to photography or the phonograph. A product label such as "electric reproducing piano" alone does not count.
The instrument remains an ordinary piano: it can be played by hand, the mechanism is invisible and leaves its look unchanged, it can be fitted to many makes of piano.
The range of music available: classics and dance music, jazz and opera, music for every mood and occasion, a library of thousands of rolls by hundreds of artists.

ab.hi:
Michael Welte
The Clockmaker of Freiburg

div.ab:
To Michael Welte,
the chiming clock-
maker of a dreamy
hamlet in Germany,
belongs the distinction
of conceiving and build-
ing an instrument that would reproduce the
actual playing of a great pianist.
Though a clock-maker by trade, Welte
was given to study and invention
and being
called on to design a musical chime for a

clock, he conceived the idea of having the
chimes play a tune.
On the accuracy and novelty of his chim-
ing clocks, Michael Welte, in 1832, founded
the firm of M. Welte & Sons, a venerable in-
stitution now located at Freiburg, Germany.
The years elapsed and Welte's clocks
chimed the passage of the hours from man-
tles in every nook of Europe, while the firm
that had begun so humbly had acquired a
continental prestige.

In 1849, after three years of patient toil,
Michael Welte brought forth his first Orches-
trion, the clumsy forerunner of the marvelous
Philharmonic Organs of the present day.
"It
was a wonder of mechanical perfection, con-
taining eleven hundred pipes, that were
brought to playing by thousands of small
pins, representing the harmonies and melo-
dies of musical compositions thus 'written'
on three large wooden cylinders, that moved
with a startling precision as had been thought
impossible before."
Many years before Edison dreamed his
thrilling dream of the phonograph the fame
of Welte's new invention had traveled
through all Europe and soon the business of
chiming clocks gave way to the making of
mechanically operated musical instruments.
Dukes and statesmen, musicians of low rank
and high rank, came from afar to listen and
marvel at Michael Welte's astounding crea-
tion. The firm expanded and the business of
M. Welte & Sons attained large proportions.
In 1865, Emil Welte, a son of the founder,

came to America where success was instan-
taneous. The demand for Welte's Orches-
trions, coming now from two hemispheres, led,
in 1872, to the removal to Freiburg, which
thus became the musical shrine of Europe.
Eight years later Michael Welte, the clock-
maker, closed his eyes forever, leaving his
sons endowed with his own inventive genius.
In 1887, Emil Welte startled the world by the
invention of a paper music-roll in connection
with a pneumatic action,
thus eliminating
the bulky wooden cylinders and giving the
instrument an unlimited repertoire.

div.p: Welte's Dream of Living Music -- A Reality

div.ab:
It was only natural that the artistic develop-
ment of Welte Orchestrions and Philhar-
monic Organs should have led the thoughts
of the Weltes onward and upward to the idea
of recording the playing of the musician
and applying to the piano a new principle
-that of reproducing the artist's playing
by means of an automatic instrument.
Thus was conceived Welte-Mignon* (pro-
nounced Well-tee Meen-yon) or "Little
Welte," as it was designated to distinguish
it from the large instruments on which

the Welte reputation and business had been
established.
Thus M. Welte & Sons were the origina-
tors of the idea of reproducing the playing of
pianists, and were granted the original, basic
patents on reproducing mechanisms now em-
ployed in the Welte-Mignon* Reproducing
Action manufactured by the Auto Pneumatic
Action Company, under a license granting
the unrestricted use of these patents in manu-
facturing reproducing actions for the piano
industry.

hi.seg: Perfect Reproduction – The Secret of Welte Mignon*

div.ab:
The Welte-Mignon* method of recording
a player's performance is photographic.
Through this
secret photographic process -
possessed only by Welte-Mignon,* available
only to Welte-Mignon* - the artist's play-
ing is actually photographed – his tempo, his
speaking notes, his dynamics,
those subtle
things that infuse an artist's very soul into
his playing.
These photographs show precisely the pres-
sure with which the artist strikes the keys,
whether ever so lightly-pianissimo-or with

the vigor of fortissimo.
And this photo-
graphic record is so perfect–so identically
the physical impression of the master's per-
formance,
that he is never called upon to edit
or arrange the recording. Thus, editing the
recording of a great pianist is not necessary
with Welte-Mignon* and only with Welte-
Mignon* is it not necessary.
Herein lies the vast difference between
Welte-Mignon* recordings of great pianists
and those of all other reproducing mechan-
isms.

Many musicians and masters whose names
gleam like stars in the firmament of music
have paid glowing tribute to Welte-Mig-
non.* From every corner of the world come
musicians to inscribe their matchless art on
the imperishable pages of Welte-Mignon's*
ever-growing library of music.
De Pach-
mann , Paderewski, Bloomfield-Zeisler,
Levy, Singer, Pouishnoff, Gieseking,
Liebling, Saar and Boguslawski are but
*Licensed under original Welte-Mignon patents

a few of the great artists whose playing you
may hear on Welte-Mignon.*
The famed Welte-Mignon* Library of in-
terpreted music is without a doubt the most
comprehensive in the world of music, con-
taining more than two thousand selections,
embracing practically every musical compo-
sition through which the master composers
of the past two centuries have immortalized
themselves.
